title: sonar2csv_shape
text:
How to use
There are three ways to use sonar2csv_shape to convert your .sl2 or .sl3 sonar files to CSV and shapefiles:

1. Command Line Interface (CLI)
After installation with uv sync, you can use the CLI tool:
uv run sonar2csv_shape input_file.sl2 output_folder/
Example:
uv run sonar2csv_shape "measurements_+765cmNAP.sl3" ./converted_data/
You can also specify a custom coordinate reference system (CRS):
uv run sonar2csv_shape input_file.sl2 output_folder/ --crs epsg:4326
Important: The filename must contain the height of the sonar instrument at the time of measurement in cmNAP format (e.g., +765cmNAP or -1050cmNAP). This is used to calculate the bottom height in mNAP.


2. Using the Jupyter Notebook
For interactive conversion and exploration, you can use the 00_convert.ipynb notebook:

Open the notebook in Jupyter
Load your sonar file and process it step by step
Customize the conversion parameters as needed

This method is ideal for: - Exploring the data before conversion - Testing different parameters - Understanding the conversion process - Batch processing multiple files with custom logic


3. Web Interface
You can spin up a web server to provide conversion capabilities to multiple users:
uv run sonar2csv_webgui
This starts a web interface at http://localhost:5001 where users can: - Upload .sl2 or .sl3 files through their browser - Automatically convert files to CSV, shapefile, and GeoPackage formats - Download the results as a ZIP file
Note: The web interface is primarily designed for server deployments where multiple users need access to the conversion tool. For local PC usage, the CLI or notebook methods are more straightforward.


Output Files
All conversion methods produce the following output files: - Shapefile (.shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, .cpg) - for use in GIS software like QGIS or ArcGIS - CSV file (.csv) - tabular data with coordinates and measurements - GeoPackage (.gpkg) - modern geospatial format
The converted data includes: - Coordinates in the specified CRS (default: RD New / Amersfoort - EPSG:28992) - Mean, minimum, and maximum water depth - Bottom height in mNAP (calculated from measurement height and water depth) - Timestamp of measurements

🤔 Can you please explain to me what the partial function does, how it does that and what its purpose is?
🤖Reply🤖 The partial function is a really useful tool from Python’s functools module. Let me break it down for you:
What it does: partial takes a function and “freezes” some of its arguments, creating a new function with those arguments pre-filled.
How it works: When you call partial(func, arg1, arg2), it returns a new function that, when called, will automatically pass arg1 and arg2 to func, along with any additional arguments you provide later.
Simple example:
def greet(greeting, name):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"
If you use partial(greet, “Hello”), you get a new function that already has “Hello” as the greeting, so you only need to provide the name later.
In your code, partial(HTMX, app=app, host=None, port=None) creates a new function where app, host, and port are already set. So when you call preview(…) later, those parameters are automatically included.

Expanation of FastHTML fasttag Titled()
Titled() is a convenience function that creates multiple HTML elements at once (a <title> tag for the browser tab and an <h1> heading for the page). Since it’s generating these elements internally, it doesn’t expose styling parameters like cls.
In contrast, components like P() and H1() are direct HTML element creators - they map one-to-one to HTML tags. This gives you full control over their attributes, including cls for styling.
The trade-off: Titled() saves you time but limits customization, while using Title() + H1() separately gives you full control but requires more code.


The difference between Titled() and Title() ft-components from FastHTML are:
Titled(title, *content): - Sets the browser tab title - Creates a visible h1 heading on the page - Returns both together
Title(title): - Only sets the browser tab title - Creates NO visible content on the page - Must be combined with other elements to show anything
The solution: When you want a browser tab title but custom heading styling, return both:
return Title("..."), YourVisibleContent(...)

sonarhome() Documentation
Purpose: Creates the main landing page for the Sonar File Converter web application, allowing users to upload .sl2/.sl3 sonar files and receive converted shapefiles, CSV, and geopackage files as a downloadable zip.
How it works:

Layout & Branding: Uses a full-height background image (WDODelta imagery) with a centered title and form, styled with Tailwind CSS utility classes.
File Upload Form: Contains a file input and submit button that:

Posts to the upload route via HTMX (hx_post=upload)
Displays results in #result div (hx_target="#result")
Shows a loading spinner during processing (hx_indicator="#spinner")
Disables the button while uploading (hx_disabled_elt="button")

HTMX over full page reload: Keeps the user on the same page; only the result area updates—better UX for a file conversion workflow.
DaisyUI + Tailwind: Provides the spinner, button styles, and file input styling with minimal custom CSS, matching the WDODelta theme defined earlier.
Separation of concerns: The upload logic lives in a separate upload() route, keeping sonarhome() focused purely on presentation.

index() route: Redirects / to /sonarhome so the app works both in production (where users expect / to work) and in SolveIt (where you can preview /sonarhome).

🤖Reply🤖
Great question! Let’s break down what’s happening and why your intuition about using cleanup.to() is actually correct.
Why hx_on__after_request with fetch() doesn’t work well here:
When you click the download link, the browser initiates a file download. The hx_on__after_request event fires after HTMX gets the response, but since it’s a file download (not an HTMX swap), the timing gets tricky. The fetch() call might execute before or while the file is still being downloaded, causing the zip to be deleted too early or the cleanup to fail.
Why your intuition is better:
You’re right that it should be simpler! However, there’s a conceptual issue: you want to clean up after the download completes, but the download link isn’t an HTMX request—it’s a regular browser download.
The solution:
You need a separate cleanup trigger. Here’s the FastHTML way:
return Div(
    P("Conversion complete!"),
    A("Download Results", href=get_file.to(fn=zip_path.name), cls='btn btn-success'),
    Button("Done", hx_post=cleanup.to(fn=zip_path.name), cls='btn btn-sm mt-2')
)
And add the cleanup route:
@rt
def cleanup(fn: str):
    (Path("/app/data") / fn).unlink(missing_ok=True)
Why this works better:

User downloads the file normally
When they’re done, they click “Done” to clean up
The cleanup happens via a proper HTMX POST request

Does this make sense? Would you like to try implementing this approach?
So there’s no way to register if the downloading is complete? It is not a good user experience to have to click done after you are done.


🤖Reply🤖
You’re absolutely right—requiring a “Done” button is poor UX. Unfortunately, detecting when a browser download completes is genuinely tricky because:

File downloads don’t fire completion events - The browser handles downloads separately from the page, so JavaScript/HTMX can’t tell when the download finishes
The response is a file, not HTML - So there’s no DOM change to hook into

Possible approaches:

Accept temporary files - Clean up old files periodically (e.g., delete files older than 1 hour via a background task)
Stream the zip directly - Generate and serve the zip without saving it to disk at all
Use a “download started” trigger - Clean up after a short delay (risky if download is slow)

The most robust solution is #2 - streaming without saving. This eliminates the cleanup problem entirely since nothing persists on disk.

I think I have a simple approach. When the download starts another function starts that just deletes all zip files older than 2 hours. We then are sure that we don’t delete the latest zip and we also are sure we don’t get 100s of zip files. So when we add to the getfile a call to a remove function that removes all old zip files.

@rt

Add a remove files function and add the line to the current get_file to call that function. We only have to remove zip files, the other files are handled in another function.


🤖Reply🤖
Great idea! That’s a pragmatic solution. Here’s the cleanup function:
def remove_old_zips():
    upload_dir = Path("/app/data")
    cutoff = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=2)
    for zip_file in upload_dir.glob("*.zip"):
        if datetime.fromtimestamp(zip_file.stat().st_mtime) < cutoff:
            zip_file.unlink(missing_ok=True)

def clean_gdf(
